newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Petrol changes do little for rural Australia.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Petrol changes do little for rural Australia.

text.p: Australia's largest petrol station chain said on Wednesday that government moves to deregulate the petroleum industry need to go further if it hopes to lower pump prices outside the big cities.
Ampol said it does not believe the objective of lower rural petrol prices can be achieved until the limits on the number of stations Ampol and other big chains can operate nationally is removed.
On average, rural consumers pay between six and 15 cents a litre more at the pump than city drivers.
Fewer outlets and less demand for non-petrol items combine to make petrol in rural Australia more costly.
On average, companies such as Ampol earn only about one cent per litre after tax on petroleum sales.
Ampol is owned equally by Caltex Australia Ltd and Pioneer International Ltd and estimates it controls 28 percent of the total petroleum products market in Australia.

The government said earlier on Wednesday it will remove controls on petrol prices, give open access to oil terminals, increase monitoring of prices and establish a fair business practice code for the oil industry as part of its mandate to deregulate the industry.
"We are pleased that the government intends to deliver on its election commitment to deregulate prices," Ampol managing director Ian Blackburne said in a statement.
"However, this is not deregulation of the petroleum industry so long as the government continues to prevent oil companies operating all but a very small number of service stations."
Australia's petrol industry is dominated by four major companies -- Ampol, BP Australia Ltd, Mobil Oil Australia Ltd and Shell Australia.
Efforts are planned to lobby the government to relax its grip on the retail sector.
"We shall be consulting with the government to seek urgent moves to accelerate the deregulation process," Jim Starkey, executive director of the Australian Institute of Petroleum, told Reuters.
"We were hoping the whole deregulation process would have been done a lot quicker," he added.
Mobil also called for further deregulation.
"Regulation in this industry is cumbersome, outdated and creates inefficiencies that the customer ends up paying for," Mobil chairman P.C. Tan said in a statement.

Despite the latest relaxing of controls, integrated oil companies such as Ampol and Mobil maintain they are still under the heavy hand of government while newcomers to the industry are given more freedom.

"As the regulatory restrictions apply only to refiner-marketers, until reform actually occurs, the regulatory regime will continue to operate in favour of Woolworths and other independent marketers," Tan said.
Retailer Woolworths Ltd said on Friday it had reached agreement with Burmah Oil to sell refined petroleum products from some Woolworths outlets in New South Wales and Victoria.
Woolworths said in August that the petrol sold from its supermarket carparks would be imported.
Another of the nation's big petrol retailers, BP, said consumers should not expect to see much difference at the pumps soon.
"Until all issues affecting dergulation are addressed, there will be little change and little benefit for the consumer," BP's managing director Ron McGimpsey said.
-- James Regan, Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
